134	## Specification Tests
135	
136	### RESET Test (Ramsey)
137	
138	Ramsey's Regression Equation Specification Error Test:
139	
140	```python
141	from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import linear_reset
142	
143	reset_result = linear_reset(results, power=3, use_f=True)
144	print(reset_result.fvalue)   # F-statistic
145	print(reset_result.pvalue)   # p-value
146	print(reset_result.df_denom) # denominator df
147	```
148	
149	- H0: model is correctly specified
150	- `power=3` adds ŷ² and ŷ³ as auxiliary regressors (default behavior)
151	- `use_f=True` returns F-statistic; `use_f=False` returns chi-squared
152	- Rejection suggests omitted variables, wrong functional form, or omitted
153	  interactions — but does not identify which
154	
155	### Harvey-Collier Test (Linearity)
156	
157	```python
158	from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import linear_harvey_collier
159	
160	t_stat, pvalue = linear_harvey_collier(results)
161	```
162	
163	- H0: relationship is linear
164	- Tests using recursive residuals — sensitive to structural breaks as well as
165	  nonlinearity

169	## Multicollinearity
170	
171	### Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)
172	
173	```python
174	from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor
175	
176	# X must include a constant column
177	X = sm.add_constant(df[["x1", "x2", "x3"]])
178	
179	vif_data = pd.DataFrame({
180	    "Variable": X.columns,
181	    "VIF": [variance_inflation_factor(X.values, i) for i in range(X.shape[1])]
182	})
183	print(vif_data)
184	```
185	
186	Interpretation thresholds:
187	- VIF = 1: no collinearity
188	- VIF > 5: moderate concern
189	- VIF > 10: serious multicollinearity
190	
191	The constant's VIF is meaningless — exclude it from display or interpretation.
192	`variance_inflation_factor` takes the full design matrix (as a numpy array)
193	and a column index; loop over column indices to compute VIF for each variable.
194	
195	### Condition Number
196	
197	```python
198	# Available directly from results object
199	print(results.condition_number)
200	
201	# Or compute manually
202	import numpy as np
203	cond = np.linalg.cond(results.model.exog)
204	```
205	
206	- Condition number > 30: potential multicollinearity concern
207	- Also reported in the bottom section of `results.summary()` output

211	## Influence Measures
212	
213	### OLSInfluence (Comprehensive)
214	
215	```python
216	from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import OLSInfluence
217	
218	influence = OLSInfluence(results)
219	
220	# Cook's distance
221	cooks_d, pvalues = influence.cooks_distance
222	# Rule of thumb: Cook's D > 4/n is influential
223	
224	# Leverage (hat matrix diagonal)
225	leverage = influence.hat_matrix_diag
226	# Rule of thumb: leverage > 2*(k+1)/n is high leverage
227	
228	# DFFITS
229	dffits = influence.dffits[0]
230	# Rule of thumb: |DFFITS| > 2*sqrt((k+1)/n)
231	
232	# DFBETAS (influence on each coefficient separately)
233	dfbetas = influence.dfbetas
234	# Shape: (n_obs, n_params)
235	# Rule of thumb: |DFBETAS| > 2/sqrt(n)
236	
237	# Externally studentized residuals
238	student_resid = influence.resid_studentized_external
239	# |studentized resid| > 2 is a potential outlier
240	```
241	
242	Where k = number of predictors (excluding constant) and n = number of
243	observations.
244	
245	### Summary Frame (All Metrics at Once)
246	
247	```python
248	summary = influence.summary_frame()
249	print(summary.columns.tolist())
250	# Includes: dfb_Intercept, dfb_x1, ..., cooks_d, standard_resid,
251	#           hat_diag, dffits_internal, student_resid
252	```
253	
254	The summary frame is the most efficient way to flag observations that exceed
255	multiple thresholds simultaneously. Filter on `cooks_d` and `hat_diag` in
256	combination to distinguish high-influence from high-leverage points.

324	## Serial Correlation
325	
326	### Durbin-Watson Statistic
327	
328	```python
329	from statsmodels.stats.stattools import durbin_watson
330	
331	dw = durbin_watson(results.resid)
332	```
333	
334	- DW ≈ 2: no autocorrelation
335	- DW < 2: positive autocorrelation (values closer to 0 = stronger)
336	- DW > 2: negative autocorrelation (values closer to 4 = stronger)
337	- Also reported in `results.summary()` output
338	- Cannot be used when the model contains a lagged dependent variable
339	
340	### Breusch-Godfrey Test
341	
342	More general than Durbin-Watson; works with lagged dependent variables:
343	
344	```python
345	from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import acorr_breusch_godfrey
346	
347	lm_stat, lm_pvalue, f_stat, f_pvalue = acorr_breusch_godfrey(
348	    results, nlags=4
349	)
350	```
351	
352	- H0: no serial correlation up to lag `nlags`
353	- `nlags` should be set based on data frequency (e.g., 4 for quarterly, 12
354	  for monthly)
355	- Returns LM statistic, LM p-value, F-statistic, F p-value
356	
357	### Ljung-Box Test
358	
359	```python
360	from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import acorr_ljungbox
361	
362	lb_result = acorr_ljungbox(results.resid, lags=10, return_df=True)
363	print(lb_result)
364	# DataFrame with columns: lb_stat, lb_pvalue
365	# One row per lag
366	```
367	
368	- H0: residuals are independently distributed up to the specified lag
369	- `return_df=True` returns results as a DataFrame indexed by lag number
370	- Primarily used for time series residuals from ARIMA models, but applicable
371	  to any regression residuals when serial correlation is a concern

145	## WLS (Weighted Least Squares)
146	
147	Use when errors have non-constant variance (heteroskedasticity) but the variance structure is known or estimable. Observations with smaller error variance receive higher weight.
148	
149	### Formula API
150	
151	```python
152	# weight = 1 / variance: high variance → low weight → less influence
153	results = smf.wls("y ~ x1 + x2", data=df, weights=1/df["variance"]).fit()
154	```
155	
156	### Array API
157	
158	```python
159	X = sm.add_constant(df[["x1", "x2"]])
160	results = sm.WLS(df["y"], X, weights=1/df["variance"]).fit()
161	```
162	
163	### Common Weight Specifications
164	
165	```python
166	# Population-weighted regression (each obs represents pop_i people)
167	results = smf.wls("y ~ x1 + x2", data=df, weights=df["population"]).fit()
168	
169	# Precision weights from measurement error variance
170	results = smf.wls("y ~ x1", data=df, weights=1/df["meas_var"]).fit()
171	
172	# Inverse of squared fitted standard deviations (feasible WLS)
173	ols_resid = smf.ols("y ~ x1", data=df).fit().resid
174	df["abs_resid"] = ols_resid.abs()
175	aux = smf.ols("abs_resid ~ x1", data=df).fit()
176	fitted_sd = aux.fittedvalues
177	results = smf.wls("y ~ x1", data=df, weights=1/fitted_sd**2).fit()
178	```
179	
180	The `weights` parameter in statsmodels WLS is the **inverse of the error variance**, not the square root. Larger weight = observation is more reliable.
181	
182	### Accessing Results
183	
184	All standard OLS result attributes apply: `.params`, `.pvalues`, `.conf_int()`, `.fittedvalues`, `.resid`, `.rsquared`, etc.
185	
186	The R² in WLS is weighted; interpret with care relative to OLS R².
187

190	## GLS (Generalized Least Squares)
191	
192	Use when errors are correlated or have non-constant variance and the full covariance structure of errors is known (or estimable).
193	
194	### Array API
195	
196	```python
197	import statsmodels.api as sm
198	import numpy as np
199	
200	X = sm.add_constant(df[["x1", "x2"]])
201	y = df["y"]
202	
203	# sigma: covariance matrix of errors (n x n)
204	results = sm.GLS(y, X, sigma=covariance_matrix).fit()
205	```
206	
207	`sigma` can be:
208	- A full `(n, n)` covariance matrix
209	- A 1-d array of length `n` for diagonal (heteroskedastic only, equivalent to WLS)
210	- `None` (falls back to OLS)
211	
212	### GLSAR for AR(p) Error Structure
213	
214	When errors follow an autoregressive process, `GLSAR` is more practical than specifying the full covariance matrix:
215	
216	```python
217	# AR(1) errors
218	results = sm.GLSAR(y, X, rho=1).fit()
219	
220	# AR(2) errors
221	results = sm.GLSAR(y, X, rho=2).fit()
222	```
223	
224	Iterative estimation (Cochrane-Orcutt / Prais-Winsten style):
225	
226	```python
227	from statsmodels.regression.linear_model import GLSAR
228	
229	model = GLSAR(y, X, rho=1)
230	results = model.iterative_fit(maxiter=10)
231	print(f"Estimated rho: {model.rho}")
232	print(results.summary())
233	```
234	
235	### GLS vs. WLS vs. GLSAR
236	
237	| Situation | Recommended |
238	|-----------|-------------|
239	| Known variance weights only | `sm.WLS` |
240	| Known full error covariance matrix | `sm.GLS` |
241	| AR(p) error autocorrelation | `sm.GLSAR` |
242	| Unknown heteroskedasticity | `sm.OLS` + robust standard errors |

246	## Robust Regression (RLM)
247	
248	M-estimators that iteratively downweight influential observations (outliers). Use when OLS residual diagnostics show influential outliers but removing them is not justified.
249	
250	### Basic Usage
251	
252	```python
253	import statsmodels.api as sm
254	
255	X = sm.add_constant(df[["x1", "x2"]])
256	y = df["y"]
257	
258	# Default: Huber's T norm
259	results = sm.RLM(y, X).fit()
260	print(results.summary())
261	```
262	
263	Formula API (via `smf`):
264	
265	```python
266	import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
267	
268	results = smf.rlm("y ~ x1 + x2", data=df).fit()
269	```
270	
271	### M-Estimator Norms
272	
273	All norms are in `sm.robust.norms`:
274	
275	```python
276	# Huber's T (default, tuning constant 1.345)
277	results = sm.RLM(y, X, M=sm.robust.norms.HuberT()).fit()
278	
279	# Tukey's biweight (fully rejects extreme outliers)
280	results = sm.RLM(y, X, M=sm.robust.norms.TukeyBiweight()).fit()
281	
282	# Andrew's wave (sinusoidal redescending)
283	results = sm.RLM(y, X, M=sm.robust.norms.AndrewWave()).fit()
284	
285	# Hampel (three-part influence function)
286	results = sm.RLM(y, X, M=sm.robust.norms.Hampel()).fit()
287	
288	# LeastSquares (equivalent to OLS — comparison baseline)
289	results = sm.RLM(y, X, M=sm.robust.norms.LeastSquares()).fit()
290	```
291	
292	| Norm | Behavior | Use When |
293	|------|----------|----------|
294	| `HuberT()` | Default; tuning constant 1.345 | General robustness |
295	| `TukeyBiweight()` | Fully rejects extreme outliers | Known heavy outliers |
296	| `AndrewWave()` | Sinusoidal redescending | Moderate outlier resistance |
297	| `Hampel()` | Three-part influence function | Flexible outlier handling |
298	| `LeastSquares()` | Equivalent to OLS | Comparison baseline |
299	
300	### Accessing Weights and Diagnostics
301	
302	```python
303	results.weights         # Per-observation weights (0 = completely downweighted)
304	results.params          # Coefficient estimates
305	results.pvalues         # P-values
306	results.conf_int()      # Confidence intervals
307	```
308	
309	Identifying downweighted observations:
310	
311	```python
312	import pandas as pd
313	
314	weight_df = pd.DataFrame({
315	    "weight": results.weights,
316	    "resid": results.resid
317	}, index=df.index)
318	
319	# Observations with weight below 0.5 are substantially downweighted
320	outliers = weight_df[weight_df["weight"] < 0.5]
321	print(f"{len(outliers)} observations downweighted below 0.5")
322	print(outliers.sort_values("weight"))
323	```
324	
325	### Comparing OLS and RLM
326	
327	```python
328	ols_res = sm.OLS(y, X).fit()
329	rlm_res = sm.RLM(y, X).fit()
330	
331	comparison = pd.DataFrame({
332	    "OLS": ols_res.params,
333	    "RLM": rlm_res.params,
334	    "diff": rlm_res.params - ols_res.params
335	})
336	print(comparison)
337	# Large differences signal that outliers are influencing OLS estimates
338	```
339	
340	---
341	
342	## Quantile Regression (QuantReg)
343	
344	Models conditional quantiles of y rather than the conditional mean. Useful for understanding distributional effects, heterogeneous treatment effects, and when outliers make OLS mean-unstable.
345	
346	### Basic Usage
347	
348	```python
349	# Formula API — median regression
350	results = smf.quantreg("y ~ x1 + x2", data=df).fit(q=0.5)
351	
352	# 25th percentile
353	results = smf.quantreg("y ~ x1 + x2", data=df).fit(q=0.25)
354	
355	# 90th percentile
356	results = smf.quantreg("y ~ x1 + x2", data=df).fit(q=0.90)
357	
358	# Array API
359	results = sm.QuantReg(y, X).fit(q=0.75)
360	```
361	
362	The `q` parameter is the quantile to estimate (0 < q < 1). `q=0.5` is least absolute deviations (LAD) regression, equivalent to median regression.
363	
364	### Standard Errors
365	
366	By default, sparsity-based asymptotic standard errors are used. Bootstrap standard errors are often preferred in practice:
367	
368	```python
369	# Kernel-based robust standard errors (default)
370	results = smf.quantreg("y ~ x1 + x2", data=df).fit(
371	    q=0.5,
372	    vcov="robust",    # default; kernel-based (Powell sandwich)
373	    kernel="epa",     # Epanechnikov kernel for sparsity estimation
374	    bandwidth="hsheather"  # bandwidth selection method
375	)
376	```
377	
378	Available kernels for bandwidth: `"epa"` (Epanechnikov), `"cos"`, `"gau"` (Gaussian), `"par"` (Parzen), `"tri"` (triangular).
379	
380	### Fitting Multiple Quantiles
381	
382	```python
383	quantiles = [0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 0.90]
384	qr_results = {}
385	
386	for q in quantiles:
387	    qr_results[q] = smf.quantreg("y ~ x1 + x2", data=df).fit(q=q)
388	
389	# Compare x1 coefficient across quantiles
390	x1_coefs = pd.Series(
391	    {q: qr_results[q].params["x1"] for q in quantiles},
392	    name="x1_coef"
393	)
394	print(x1_coefs)
395	```
396	
397	### Accessing Results
398	
399	All standard result attributes apply:
400	
401	```python
402	results.params
403	results.pvalues
404	results.conf_int()
405	results.fittedvalues
406	results.resid
407	results.predict(new_data)
408	```
409	
410	Pseudo R² (Koenker-Machado):
411	
412	```python
413	results.prsquared   # 1 - sum(check_loss) / sum(check_loss_null)
414	```
415	
416	---
417	
418	## Polynomial and Spline Regression
419	
420	### Polynomial Terms via `I()`
421	
422	The `I()` wrapper in patsy formulas passes the expression through as raw Python, bypassing formula operator interpretation:
423	
424	```python
425	# Quadratic (degree 2)
426	results = smf.ols("y ~ x1 + I(x1**2)", data=df).fit()
427	
428	# Cubic (degree 3)
429	results = smf.ols("y ~ x1 + I(x1**2) + I(x1**3)", data=df).fit()
430	
431	# Interaction with polynomial
432	results = smf.ols("y ~ x1 + I(x1**2) + x2 + x1:x2", data=df).fit()
433	```
434	
435	In the array API, add polynomial columns to the DataFrame manually:
436	
437	```python
438	X = pd.DataFrame({
439	    "x1": df["x1"],
440	    "x1_sq": df["x1"] ** 2,
441	    "x1_cu": df["x1"] ** 3,
442	    "x2": df["x2"]
443	})
444	X = sm.add_constant(X)
445	results = sm.OLS(df["y"], X).fit()
446	```
447	
448	### B-Spline Basis via patsy `bs()`
449	
450	```python
451	from patsy import bs
452	
453	# Cubic B-spline with 4 degrees of freedom (1 intercept + 3 basis functions)
454	results = smf.ols("y ~ bs(x1, df=4, degree=3)", data=df).fit()
455	
456	# Natural spline with knots at specific values
457	results = smf.ols("y ~ bs(x1, knots=[25, 50, 75], degree=3)", data=df).fit()
458	
459	# Spline without intercept (no separate constant in the spline)
460	results = smf.ols("y ~ bs(x1, df=5, degree=3, include_intercept=False)", data=df).fit()
461	```
462	
463	`df` (degrees of freedom): number of basis functions, equal to `degree + number_of_interior_knots`. Knot locations default to quantiles of x1.
464	
465	`degree`:
466	- 1 = piecewise linear
467	- 2 = piecewise quadratic
468	- 3 = cubic (most common, C2 continuity)
469	
470	Generating the spline basis for prediction or inspection:
471	
472	```python
473	from patsy import dmatrix
474	
475	# Fit on training data
476	basis_train = dmatrix("bs(x1, df=4, degree=3)", data=df, return_type="dataframe")
477	results = sm.OLS(df["y"], basis_train).fit()
478	
479	# Apply same transformation to new data
480	basis_new = dmatrix("bs(x1, df=4, degree=3)", data=new_df, return_type="dataframe")
481	y_pred = results.predict(basis_new)
482	```
483	
484	Using `dmatrix` ensures knot locations from training are reused at prediction time.
485	
486	---
487	
488	## Interaction Terms
489	
490	### Formula API Operators
491	
492	| Operator | Meaning | Equivalent to |
493	|----------|---------|---------------|
494	| `x1 * x2` | Full interaction (main effects + interaction) | `x1 + x2 + x1:x2` |
495	| `x1 : x2` | Interaction term only (no main effects) | product of x1 and x2 |
496	| `(x1 + x2 + x3)**2` | All pairwise interactions | `x1 + x2 + x3 + x1:x2 + x1:x3 + x2:x3` |
497	
498	```python
499	# Full interaction
500	results = smf.ols("y ~ x1 * x2", data=df).fit()
501	
502	# Interaction term only (suppresses main effects)
503	results = smf.ols("y ~ x1:x2", data=df).fit()
504	
505	# Categorical interaction — C() marks a column as categorical
506	results = smf.ols("y ~ x1 * C(group)", data=df).fit()
507	
508	# Three-way interaction (all lower-order terms included)
509	results = smf.ols("y ~ x1 * x2 * x3", data=df).fit()
510	
511	# All pairwise interactions among three variables
512	results = smf.ols("y ~ (x1 + x2 + x3)**2", data=df).fit()
513	```
514	
515	### Categorical Reference Level
516	
517	By default, patsy uses the first category alphabetically as the reference level. Override:
518	
519	```python
520	# Set "control" as the reference level
521	results = smf.ols("y ~ x1 * C(group, Treatment('control'))", data=df).fit()
522	```
523	
524	### Array API — Manual Interaction Columns
525	
526	```python
527	X = df[["x1", "x2"]].copy()
528	X["x1_x2"] = X["x1"] * X["x2"]   # continuous × continuous
529	
530	# Continuous × categorical (dummy)
531	X["treat"] = (df["group"] == "treatment").astype(int)
532	X["x1_treat"] = X["x1"] * X["treat"]
533	
534	X = sm.add_constant(X)
535	results = sm.OLS(df["y"], X).fit()
536	```
537	
538	### Interpreting Interaction Coefficients
539	
540	```python
541	results = smf.ols("y ~ x1 * x2", data=df).fit()
542	
543	# Coefficient on x1:x2 is the marginal effect of x1 on y
544	# per unit increase in x2 (and vice versa)
545	print(results.params)
546	print(results.conf_int())
547	
548	# For categorical interactions: the coefficient on x1:C(group)[T.treated]
549	# is the difference in the x1 slope between treated and reference groups
550	```
551	
552	---
553	
554	## Mixed Effects / Multilevel Models (MixedLM)
555	
556	For hierarchical/nested data (e.g., students in schools, repeated measures):
557	
558	```python
559	import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
560	
561	# Random intercept model (varying intercept by group)
562	results = smf.mixedlm(
563	    "score ~ ses + school_type",
564	    data=df,
565	    groups=df["school_id"]
566	).fit()
567	print(results.summary())
568	
569	# Random intercept + random slope
570	results = smf.mixedlm(
571	    "score ~ ses + school_type",
572	    data=df,
573	    groups=df["school_id"],
574	    re_formula="~ses"           # ses has a random slope by school
575	).fit()
576	```
577	
578	Array API:
579	```python
580	import statsmodels.api as sm
581	
582	model = sm.MixedLM(
583	    endog=y,
584	    exog=X,                     # fixed effects design matrix
585	    groups=groups,              # grouping variable
586	    exog_re=Z                   # random effects design matrix
587	)
588	results = model.fit()
589	```
590	
591	Key parameters:
592	- `groups`: grouping variable defining the clusters (e.g., school ID, subject ID)
593	- `re_formula`: formula for random effects (default: random intercept only, `"~1"`)
594	- `vc_formula`: variance components formula for crossed random effects
595	
596	Results attributes:
597	- `results.fe_params` — fixed effects coefficients
598	- `results.random_effects` — dict of random effects by group
599	- `results.cov_re` — random effects covariance matrix
600	- `results.bse_fe` — standard errors for fixed effects
601	- `results.bse_re` — standard errors for random effects variance components
602	
603	Prediction:
604	```python
605	# Fixed effects prediction (population average)
606	pred = results.predict(new_data)
607	
608	# Group-specific prediction (includes random effects)
609	pred = results.predict(new_data, exog_re=new_Z)
610	```
611	
612	Common use cases in education research:
613	- Students nested in classrooms nested in schools (two-level or three-level)
614	- Repeated test scores for the same student over time (longitudinal)
615	- Schools nested in districts with district-level predictors
616	
617	Convergence: MixedLM uses gradient-based optimization by default (BFGS, L-BFGS-B, CG sequence). For convergence issues, try:
618	```python
619	results = model.fit(method=["powell"])     # Powell optimizer
620	results = model.fit(maxiter=200)           # Increase max iterations
621	results = model.fit(reml=False)            # ML instead of REML
622	```

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Stage 8.1: Hierarchical OLS regression -- selectivity vs. effectiveness.

Task: regression-models
Wave: 9, Step: 6, Stage: 8
Depends on: create-bands (Stage 7)
Input: data/processed/2026-03-29_analysis.parquet
Output: output/analysis/2026-03-29_regression_results.parquet
Checkpoint: CP4

Research Question: How much of the variation in college graduation rates is
attributable to institutional selectivity versus institutional effectiveness?

Models:
  Model 1: completion_rate_150pct ~ admit_rate
  Model 2: Model 1 + pell_share + urm_share
  Model 3: Model 2 + student_faculty_ratio + retention_rate + log_instr_expend
  Model 3b: Model 3 + C(inst_control)
All estimated with HC1 robust standard errors.
"""

import polars as pl
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from pathlib import Path

# --- Config ---
# Configuration constants from Plan Section 5 (Analysis Design).
# Four hierarchical OLS models test whether selectivity (admit_rate) explains
# graduation rates beyond what student composition and institutional resources explain.
PROJECT_DIR = Path("/daaf/research/2026-03-29_College_Graduation_Rate_Selectivity_Analysis")
DATE_PREFIX = "2026-03-29"

INPUT_PATH = PROJECT_DIR / "data" / "processed" / f"{DATE_PREFIX}_analysis.parquet"
OUTPUT_PATH = PROJECT_DIR / "output" / "analysis" / f"{DATE_PREFIX}_regression_results.parquet"

# Analysis variables from Plan specification
OUTCOME = "completion_rate_150pct"
KEY_PREDICTOR = "admit_rate"
COMPOSITION_VARS = ["pell_share", "urm_share"]
RESOURCE_VARS = ["student_faculty_ratio", "retention_rate", "instr_expend_per_fte"]
SECTOR_VAR = "inst_control"

# All variables needed for complete-case analysis (Model 3 requires all seven)
ALL_ANALYSIS_VARS = [OUTCOME, KEY_PREDICTOR] + COMPOSITION_VARS + RESOURCE_VARS

# --- Load ---
# Load the analysis dataset built in Stage 7 and verify shape.
print("=" * 60)
print("Stage 8.1: Hierarchical OLS Regression")
print("=" * 60)

df = pl.read_parquet(INPUT_PATH)
print(f"Loaded: {df.shape[0]:,} rows x {df.shape[1]} cols")

# --- Pre-state ---
# Verify all required analysis variables exist and document missingness.
pre_rows = df.shape[0]

missing_vars = [v for v in ALL_ANALYSIS_VARS + [SECTOR_VAR] if v not in df.columns]
assert not missing_vars, f"STOP: Missing analysis variables: {missing_vars}"

print(f"\nPre-state: {pre_rows:,} rows")
print("\nMissingness by analysis variable:")
for var in ALL_ANALYSIS_VARS + [SECTOR_VAR]:
    null_ct = df[var].null_count()
    null_pct = null_ct / pre_rows * 100
    print(f"  {var}: {null_ct:,} nulls ({null_pct:.1f}%)")

# --- Complete-Case Dataset ---
# INTENT: Create a single complete-case dataset across ALL seven continuous
# analysis variables so that Models 1-3b are estimated on the SAME sample.
# This ensures R-squared changes reflect added predictors, not sample changes.
#
# REASONING: Listwise deletion across all Model 3 variables is the appropriate
# strategy here because (a) we need consistent samples for hierarchical model
# comparison, and (b) the main driver of missingness is admit_rate (open-admission
# institutions have no admission rate), which is the key predictor -- imputation
# of the key predictor would undermine the research question.
#
# ASSUMES: Missingness is primarily driven by open-admission institutions lacking
# admit_rate data. The Plan documents this as ~54% complete-case rate (~1,058 rows).
df_complete = df.drop_nulls(subset=ALL_ANALYSIS_VARS)
complete_n = df_complete.shape[0]
dropped = pre_rows - complete_n
drop_pct = dropped / pre_rows * 100

print(f"\nComplete-case dataset: {complete_n:,} rows")
print(f"Dropped: {dropped:,} rows ({drop_pct:.1f}%)")
print(f"NOTE: High drop rate ({drop_pct:.1f}%) is expected and documented in Plan.")
print("  Primary driver: admit_rate nulls (open-admission institutions).")

# --- Log-Transform Finance Variable ---
# INTENT: Log-transform instr_expend_per_fte before entering Models 3/3b.
# REASONING: The raw variable has extreme outliers (up to $14.1M/FTE from
# Wave 8 correlation analysis). Log-transformation compresses the right tail,
# stabilizes variance, and allows coefficient interpretation as elasticity-like
# (percentage change in spending associated with graduation rate change).
# Using np.log1p (log(1+x)) to safely handle any zero values.
# ASSUMES: instr_expend_per_fte >= 0 for all observations.
df_complete = df_complete.with_columns(
    pl.col("instr_expend_per_fte").map_batches(
        lambda s: pl.Series(np.log1p(s.to_numpy().astype(float)))
    ).alias("log_instr_expend")
)

print(f"\nLog-transformed instr_expend_per_fte -> log_instr_expend")
log_vals = df_complete["log_instr_expend"]
print(f"  Range: [{log_vals.min():.3f}, {log_vals.max():.3f}]")
print(f"  Mean: {log_vals.mean():.3f}, Median: {log_vals.median():.3f}")

# --- Convert to Pandas for statsmodels ---
# REASONING: statsmodels formula API requires pandas DataFrames.
# Converting only the complete-case subset (not the full dataset).
pdf = df_complete.to_pandas()

# Ensure inst_control is treated as categorical
# ASSUMES: inst_control values are 1=public, 2=private NP, 3=for-profit
pdf["inst_control"] = pdf["inst_control"].astype(int)

print(f"\nSample for regression: {len(pdf):,} rows")
print(f"inst_control distribution:")
print(pdf["inst_control"].value_counts().sort_index().to_string())

# --- Model Estimation ---
# INTENT: Estimate four hierarchical OLS models to decompose how much of the
# graduation rate variation is explained by selectivity alone (Model 1), student
# composition (Model 2), institutional resources (Model 3), and sector (Model 3b).
# All models use HC1 robust standard errors to address heteroskedasticity.
#
# REASONING: Hierarchical (nested) model specification is standard for assessing
# incremental explanatory power. HC1 is used per the Plan specification and is
# the default robust SE choice for cross-sectional data (White 1980).

print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("MODEL ESTIMATION (HC1 Robust SEs)")
print("=" * 60)

# Model 1: Selectivity only
# INTENT: Baseline model -- how much does selectivity alone explain?
m1 = smf.ols(
    f"{OUTCOME} ~ {KEY_PREDICTOR}",
    data=pdf
).fit(cov_type="HC1")
print(f"\nModel 1 (Selectivity only): R2={m1.rsquared:.4f}, Adj.R2={m1.rsquared_adj:.4f}, N={int(m1.nobs)}")

# Model 2: Add student composition
# INTENT: Does adding Pell share and URM share improve explanation?
m2 = smf.ols(
    f"{OUTCOME} ~ {KEY_PREDICTOR} + {' + '.join(COMPOSITION_VARS)}",
    data=pdf
).fit(cov_type="HC1")
print(f"Model 2 (+Composition):    R2={m2.rsquared:.4f}, Adj.R2={m2.rsquared_adj:.4f}, N={int(m2.nobs)}")

# Model 3: Add institutional resources
# INTENT: Full model with selectivity + composition + resources.
# Uses log_instr_expend instead of raw instr_expend_per_fte.
m3 = smf.ols(
    f"{OUTCOME} ~ {KEY_PREDICTOR} + {' + '.join(COMPOSITION_VARS)} + student_faculty_ratio + retention_rate + log_instr_expend",
    data=pdf
).fit(cov_type="HC1")
print(f"Model 3 (+Resources):      R2={m3.rsquared:.4f}, Adj.R2={m3.rsquared_adj:.4f}, N={int(m3.nobs)}")

# Model 3b: Add sector dummies
# INTENT: Does sector (public/private NP/for-profit) explain additional variation
# beyond selectivity, composition, and resources?
# REASONING: C(inst_control) creates treatment-coded dummies. Default reference
# is the lowest value (1 = public).
m3b = smf.ols(
    f"{OUTCOME} ~ {KEY_PREDICTOR} + {' + '.join(COMPOSITION_VARS)} + student_faculty_ratio + retention_rate + log_instr_expend + C(inst_control)",
    data=pdf
).fit(cov_type="HC1")
print(f"Model 3b (+Sector):        R2={m3b.rsquared:.4f}, Adj.R2={m3b.rsquared_adj:.4f}, N={int(m3b.nobs)}")

# --- R-squared Change ---
# INTENT: Compute incremental R-squared to quantify the explanatory contribution
# of each variable block (composition and resources).
# REASONING: R2 change from Model 1->2 measures the added value of knowing
# student composition beyond selectivity. R2 change from Model 2->3 measures
# the added value of institutional resources beyond selectivity and composition.
r2_change_1to2 = m2.rsquared - m1.rsquared
r2_change_2to3 = m3.rsquared - m2.rsquared
r2_change_3to3b = m3b.rsquared - m3.rsquared

print(f"\nR-squared Changes:")
print(f"  Model 1 -> 2 (student composition): +{r2_change_1to2:.4f}")
print(f"  Model 2 -> 3 (resources):           +{r2_change_2to3:.4f}")
print(f"  Model 3 -> 3b (sector):             +{r2_change_3to3b:.4f}")

# --- H2 Assessment ---
# INTENT: Test H2 -- Does the admit_rate coefficient attenuate substantially
# from Model 1 to Model 3 when composition and resources are added?
# REASONING: If selectivity is merely proxying for composition and resources,
# the admit_rate coefficient should shrink substantially. If it retains much
# of its magnitude, selectivity has an independent association with graduation.
admit_coef_m1 = m1.params[KEY_PREDICTOR]
admit_coef_m2 = m2.params[KEY_PREDICTOR]
admit_coef_m3 = m3.params[KEY_PREDICTOR]
admit_coef_m3b = m3b.params[KEY_PREDICTOR]

attenuation_m1_to_m3 = (admit_coef_m1 - admit_coef_m3) / admit_coef_m1 * 100

print(f"\n{'=' * 60}")
print("H2 ASSESSMENT: Admit Rate Coefficient Attenuation")
print(f"{'=' * 60}")
print(f"  Model 1 (selectivity only):  {admit_coef_m1:.4f}")
print(f"  Model 2 (+composition):      {admit_coef_m2:.4f}")
print(f"  Model 3 (+resources):        {admit_coef_m3:.4f}")
print(f"  Model 3b (+sector):          {admit_coef_m3b:.4f}")
print(f"  Attenuation M1->M3: {attenuation_m1_to_m3:.1f}%")

if abs(attenuation_m1_to_m3) > 50:
    print(f"  FINDING: admit_rate coefficient attenuated by {attenuation_m1_to_m3:.1f}% -- substantial.")
    print("  Selectivity's association is largely mediated by composition/resources.")
else:
    print(f"  FINDING: admit_rate coefficient attenuated by {attenuation_m1_to_m3:.1f}% -- moderate.")
    print("  Selectivity retains independent association beyond composition/resources.")

# --- Formatted Regression Table ---
# INTENT: Print a comprehensive regression table to stdout for the audit trail.
print(f"\n{'=' * 60}")
print("REGRESSION TABLE")
print(f"{'=' * 60}")

models = {"Model 1": m1, "Model 2": m2, "Model 3": m3, "Model 3b": m3b}

# Collect all variable names across models
all_vars = []
for m in models.values():
    for v in m.params.index:
        if v not in all_vars:
            all_vars.append(v)

# Print header
header = f"{'Variable':<30}"
for name in models:
    header += f" {name:>14}"
print(header)
print("-" * (30 + 15 * len(models)))

# Print coefficients with significance stars
for var in all_vars:
    row = f"{var:<30}"
    for name, m in models.items():
        if var in m.params.index:
            coef = m.params[var]
            se = m.bse[var]
            pval = m.pvalues[var]
            stars = "***" if pval < 0.001 else "**" if pval < 0.01 else "*" if pval < 0.05 else ""
